newsitem.title: USA: Britain to seek lower U.S trade barriers - diplomat.
newsitem.headline: Britain to seek lower U.S trade barriers - diplomat.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair will urge U.S. President Bill Clinton at this week's Group of Seven summit to help lower trade barriers in the transportation, energy and telecommunications industries, Britain's U.S. Ambassador said on Monday.

While the meeting with Russian President Boris Yeltsin will dominate the summit of leaders from the seven leading industrialised nations, Britain hopes to move free trade issues to the forefront, Britain's ambassador to the United States, Sir John Kerr, told reporters in Miami.
"Nobody is making the case for free trade very clearly now," Kerr said. "It's a pity that there isn't a constructive debate now."

Among Britain's top concern are U.S. laws that bar foreign ownership of telecommunications companies, restrictions on energy and financial services and laws that prevent foreign airlines from landing in the United States, picking up passengers and flying on to other U.S. destination, Kerr said.
"I can't see why the Telecommunications Act should still have left the barrier on foreign ownership," Kerr said, noting that 44 American telecommunications companies operate in Britain.

U.S. consumers stand to gain if those air routes and communications services are opened to foreign competitiion, Kerr said. "We think it's done us good," Kerr said. "We think it might also do America good."

Kerr said current trade barriers keep the United States from exporting what he described as "your high-tech economy par excellence," and limit potential growth in industries that create high-paying jobs for Americans.
By contrast, he said, "The jobs that are lost in America because of free trade are relatively lower wages. Free trade is a good deal for the American worker."
Kerr was in Miami to address the Greater Miami Chamber of Commerce and the British American Chambers of Commerce of Florida.

Kerr urged the United States not to revoke China's most-favoured-nation trade status, despite the need to press for improvements in human rights issues. Doing so would be "a very damaging move" to Hong Kong, which acts as the gateway for Chinese trade, he said.
"It would be a great blow to Hong Kong," Kerr said. "There will be 2-1/2 percentage points knocked out of Hong Kong's five percent growth rate."
